---
title: "Four Queens: Convert a Chessboard into Equations"
description: "A rigorous but beginner-friendly mathematical explanation from the Algorithmic Puzzles study path."
---

## 1. Understand the situation

Put one queen in each column of a 4-by-4 chessboard, ensuring that no two share a row or diagonal. Rather than moving physical pieces around randomly, record the ROW selected in each COLUMN.

## 2. Try the smallest useful observation

Represent a placement by a row list q=[2,4,1,3]. That means columns 1–4 have queens in rows 2,4,1,3 respectively. Each row is used once, so horizontal attacks are impossible.

## 3. Write the mathematics

$$
q_i\ne q_j\quad\land\quad |q_i-q_j|\ne|i-j|\qquad(i\ne j)
$$

**Explain every symbol:** q_i is the row of the queen in column i; i and j are two different column indices. The first condition says their rows differ. The absolute-value bars calculate distance without a sign. The second condition says vertical distance cannot equal horizontal distance; otherwise the queens share a diagonal.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Compare columns 1 and 2. Their row numbers are 2 and 4, so |2−4|=2, while their column distance is |1−2|=1. Since 2≠1, these two queens do not attack diagonally. Compare columns 1 and 3: |2−1|=1 but |1−3|=2, also safe. Checking all six column pairs validates the arrangement.

## 4. Why the solution follows

A queen attacks horizontally when row numbers are equal. It attacks diagonally when the absolute row difference equals the column difference. Since our representation already places exactly one queen per column, these two tests cover every possible attack. This makes the mathematical condition both necessary and sufficient.

## 5. Work through the answer

The row arrangement [2,4,1,3] produces:

~~~text
. . Q .   row 1
Q . . .   row 2
. . . Q   row 3
. Q . .   row 4
1 2 3 4   columns
~~~

A backtracking solver assigns q_1 first, then q_2, and so on. The moment a partial list violates either inequality, every completion of that partial list is impossible, so the entire branch can be discarded.

## 6. Generalise the idea

For an n-by-n board, choose n row numbers q_1,...,q_n, one per column, and require the same inequalities for every distinct pair. The number of naive row permutations is n!, but pruning conflicts avoids exploring them all.

## 7. Your turn

Try q=[1,3,2,4]. Columns 2 and 3 differ by 1 in both row and column. Which two queens attack?

**Mathematical tools:** Constraint satisfaction, absolute values, backtracking and pruning.

**Source:** Anany and Maria Levitin, *Algorithmic Puzzles* (Oxford University Press, 2011), Tutorial puzzle (n-Queens), printed pp. 6–8.. The wording, mathematical explanations and walkthroughs here are independently written.
